hook: Twelve small security challenges inside a made-up freight company. Decode notes, audit passwords, read logs and catch a pretext call to find each flag, then pick the patch that fixes the hole it came from.
outcome: Find weaknesses in passwords, encodings, people and logs by careful reading, then recommend the fix and explain its tradeoff
sources: CSTA K-12 Computer Science Standards (2026 ids HS-SYS-SE-31, HS-SYS-SE-32, HS-SYS-SE-33; 2017 3A-NI-05 to 3A-NI-08, 3B-NI-04): https://csteachers.org/k12standards/

NIST SP 800-63B-4, section 3.1.1.2 (block common and breached passwords, allow 64+ characters and spaces, no composition rules, no forced changes, salted hashes, limit failed attempts): https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html
UK National Cyber Security Centre, Most hacked passwords revealed (2019): https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/news/most-hacked-passwords-revealed
EFF, Dice-Generated Passphrases (7,776 words, 12.9 bits per word): https://www.eff.org/dice
CISA, More than a Password and Implementing Phishing-Resistant MFA (2022): https://www.cisa.gov/MFA
RFC 4648, Base64 (an encoding with no key): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4648
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 (key management: keep keys apart from data): https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/57/pt1/r5/final
Khan Academy, Cryptography (Caesar and Vigenere ciphers): https://www.khanacademy.org/computing/computer-science/cryptography
CISA, Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks: https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/avoiding-social-engineering-and-phishing-attacks
FBI IC3, Business Email Compromise: https://www.ic3.gov
Reserved example domains, RFC 2606 and RFC 6761: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2606
Bits, guessing times and encrypted strings computed in Python (bits = length x log2 pool; time = 2 to the power of bits / 10 billion a second, a model rate stated on screen)
Larkspur Freight, its people, logs and messages are made up for Curio Class; everything is drawn in code
